"You're always watching," Tanuja said, bouncing the ball near the bench. "Want to play dodgeball?"
Jatin shrugged. "Nobody asked."
"I'm asking now."
"What if I get out first? What if I throw wrong and everyone laughs?"
"Then you get out first. I got out first yesterday. Nobody cared."
Jatin looked at the circle of shouting kids. "I don't know the rules properly."
"Stand next to me. I'll tell you as we go."
"Just one round?"
"Just one."
He stood, wiped his hands on his shorts and followed her. At the end of the round he was still in, grinning. "Again?"

qa.a: She got out first yesterday.

qa.q: What was Jatin worried about before joining?
qa.a: He worried he'd get out first or throw wrong and everyone would laugh.

qa.q: What bridge did Tanuja offer, and why did it work?
qa.a: She invited him, let him stand next to her and promised to explain the rules, making the first step small and safe.

qa.q: How might Tanuja feel when Jatin asks "Again?"
qa.a: She may feel glad and a little proud that her invitation worked.

grounding: A boy who longs to join a game but waits to be asked is helped in by a classmate's friendly invitation.

subtype: Wanting to join but holding back [Actor]
passage:
All through Class 5, I watched the lane cricket from our gate. I knew every player's name and who bowled fast. I wanted to play so badly that I practised bowling against our wall at night. But I never asked. I was sure I'd say something stupid, or they'd say no, and then I'd have to walk past them every day. Then Vijay, who lived two houses down, came to the gate one evening. "You're the one who bowls against the wall, na? We need a bowler." I followed, heart thudding. My first ball was a wide. Nobody laughed. My third ball took a wicket. Now I'm in Class 6. I still get nervous sometimes, but I ask. "Can I bat next?" It gets easier every time.
Ramesh

qa.q: Where did Ramesh practise bowling at night?
qa.a: Against the wall at home, at night.

qa.q: What worried Ramesh about asking to play?
qa.a: Ramesh was sure of saying something stupid or being refused, and then having to walk past the players every day.

qa.q: What turning point came when Vijay came to the gate?
qa.a: Vijay invited Ramesh as a needed bowler, a friendly bridge; after that, with practice, asking got easier.

qa.q: How might the other players have seen Ramesh after the wicket?
qa.a: They may have seen a useful new bowler, not the quiet kid at the gate.

grounding: A child who longed to join lane cricket but waited to be invited remembers how a neighbour's invitation and practice eased the shyness.

Monday. At recess Tenzin stood by the wall with a tennis ball in his pocket, watching the football game. He practised the words in his head: Can I play? He didn't say them.
Wednesday. Rehana, who sat beside him in class, jogged over. 'We need a goalkeeper. Want to?' Tenzin nodded before he could think. He saved one shot and laughed too loudly, then worried all afternoon that he'd looked silly.
The next Monday. Tenzin walked up to the game himself. His heart thumped. 'Can I play?' 'Obviously,' said Rehana. 'Goal's yours.'

qa.q: What did Tenzin keep in his pocket?
qa.a: A tennis ball.

qa.q: What was Tenzin worried about on Wednesday afternoon?
qa.a: He felt anxious that laughing too loudly had made him look silly.

qa.q: What helped Tenzin ask to play by the next Monday?
qa.a: Rehana's friendly invitation gave him a safe first go, and that practice made asking for himself feel possible.

qa.q: Why might Rehana have invited Tenzin?
qa.a: Rehana may have noticed him watching by the wall and guessed he wanted to join but was waiting to be asked.

grounding: Shows a child who longs to join a game but waits to be invited, is helped by a peer's friendly bridge, and grows braver with practice.

passage: Damini, you think you're the only one who waits at the edge? When your Sangeeta Mausi was ten, in Nashik, the girls played kho-kho every evening on the temple ground. I wanted to play so badly my feet itched. But I sat under the neem tree, pretending to read, waiting for someone to call me. I kept thinking, what if I run the wrong way, what if they laugh? A whole month of evenings. Then a girl called Kusum walked over and dropped her dupatta in my lap. 'Hold this for me, and then you're on my team.' I played badly that day. Nobody laughed. By Diwali I was the one calling the new girls in.

qa.a: Under the neem tree, pretending to read.

qa.q: What was young Sangeeta worried about?
qa.a: She was anxious that she would run the wrong way and the girls would laugh.

qa.q: What turning point let Sangeeta join the game?
qa.a: Kusum walking over, handing her the dupatta and putting her on the team, a friendly bridge into the game.

qa.q: Why might Kusum have walked over?
qa.a: Kusum probably noticed Sangeeta watching every evening and guessed she wanted to play.

grounding: Shows, in an elder's memory, a child who longed to join a game but waited to be invited, until a peer offered a friendly bridge.

subtype: Wanting to join but holding back [Actor]
passage: Jaya had joined the school in November, halfway through the year, and on the first rainy day recess moved indoors. Four girls were playing carrom at the back table, laughing. Jaya wanted to play so much it ached. But all four seats were taken, and what would she even say? 'Can I have next game?' sounded pushy; 'I'm good at carrom' sounded like showing off. She sat at her desk sharpening a pencil that was already sharp. Irawati, striker in hand, looked up. 'You play?' Jaya's cheeks went hot. 'A little.' Irawati shifted her chair. 'Squeeze in, be my partner. I'm terrible at the red.' Jaya perched on the edge of the chair. By the end of recess she had pocketed the red twice, and said four whole sentences.

qa.q: What was Jaya doing while the others played?
qa.a: Sharpening a pencil that was already sharp.

qa.q: What was Jaya worried about before Irawati spoke?
qa.a: She was anxious that anything she said would sound pushy or like showing off.

qa.q: What made Irawati's invitation work so well?
qa.a: It was casual and made room without pressure, and asking Jaya to be her partner offered a friendly bridge into the game.

qa.q: What might Irawati have noticed about Jaya?
qa.a: Irawati may have noticed the new girl watching the game and guessed she wanted to join.

grounding: Shows a new child longing to join a game but holding back for fear of saying the wrong thing, until a peer makes room.

subtype: Wanting to join but holding back [Actor]
passage:
Every evening the colony kids played seven stones in the lane behind Block C. Ganga watched from the steps with her chin on her knees.
She knew the rules by heart. She even knew Pinky always aimed too high. But what if she asked and they said no? What if she threw and missed everything?
On Thursday the ball rolled right to her feet. She held it, heart thumping.
Harish jogged over. "Good catch. You want to play? We need one more on our side."
Ganga nodded, cheeks hot. Her first throw missed. Harish just said, "Next one."
Her second throw knocked down three stones. Nobody made a big fuss. They just yelled, "Run!" and she ran.
The next evening, she walked straight down from the steps.

qa.q: Where did the colony kids play seven stones?
qa.a: In the lane behind Block C.

qa.q: What was Ganga worried about while she watched?
qa.a: She felt anxious that they would say no if she asked, or that she would throw and miss everything.

qa.q: What did Harish do that made it easier for Ganga to join?
qa.a: He invited her with a simple reason, "We need one more on our side," and when she missed he just said "Next one" instead of teasing.

qa.q: What would change if nobody had invited Ganga?
qa.a: She might have kept watching from the steps, longing to play but waiting, and her worry about saying or doing the wrong thing could have grown.

grounding: Shows a child who longs to join a game but waits to be invited, and how a peer's friendly bridge and a safe try ease her shyness.
